narration.text: Here are six hundred dots, scattered completely at random. Now let each one wander. Each step adds a random kick and a drift: the current position divided by two, plus the score. The green arrows show only score directions, with their lengths rescaled. Watch what the randomness builds.
narration.raw: Here are six hundred dots, scattered completely at random. <bookmark mark='a'/> Now let each one wander. Each step adds a random kick and a drift: the current position divided by two, plus the score. The green arrows show only score directions, with their lengths rescaled. <bookmark mark='b'/> Watch what the randomness builds.

narration.text: This is, in miniature, how today's image and video generators work. They start from noise and let it flow, one random step at a time, into a picture. Here the score is computed exactly from our toy letter distribution. A generative model learns the score component; the other drift term is already known. We'll build it in part twenty-one.

narration.text: Run it the other way, with the arrows gone, and the letters dissolve back into noise. Both directions are random motion, and the same mathematics describes them.

narration.text: The mathematics is older than computers. It began in 1654, in letters between Pascal and Fermat about splitting the stakes of an unfinished game. Bernoulli proved that averages settle; de Moivre found the bell curve; Bayes and Laplace reasoned from effects back to causes; Gauss fitted orbits. Einstein explained the jiggling of pollen, Fisher made likelihood the way to fit models, and Ito gave random motion its own calculus. At Los Alamos the first computers were set to sampling, and today the same ideas choose a chatbot's every word and turn noise into pictures.

narration.text: This is Part 5 of AI, Built, the last of the foundations. In it: why sums are bell-shaped, in one dimension and many; fitting, precision and belief; how far averages stray; drawing samples, and how a language model picks a word; Markov chains and Monte Carlo; and random motion, with a calculus of its own. Every result is computed here, on a laptop.
